newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 17.

text.p: National list MP Jim Gerard on Monday accepted Prime Minister Jim Bolger's offer of a plum posting as the new high commissioner to Canada as compensation for being sidelined from the job of Speaker. Gerard's resignation means Wellington lawyer and accountant Annabel Young will become a National MP. Under MMP, there is no election when a list MP resigns. Labour foreign affairs spokesman Mike Moore said Gerard's new position had "nothing" to do with advancing New Zealand's interests in Canada. "...the first appointment is political and reeks of sleaze," Moore said. Page 1.

Treasurer Winston Peters has won another round in his tussle to turn the treasurer's job into the powerhouse economic position in government, beating off a move to split responsibility for the Treasury. It is understood Finance Minister Bill Birch's access to the Treasury will be through the treasurer, and that Treasury secretary Murray Horn will be answerable solely to Peters. However, Birch will have guaranteed access to Treasury information. Coalition sources were reluctant to talk about the issue on Monday, calling it a delicate matter and one that had been the subject of considerable discussion.

But a push by Birch and other National ministers to split the responsibility for the Treasury between the treasurer and the finance minister failed when NZ First expressed strong concern about that arrangement. Page 1.

Brierley Investments has made another move into the media, this time in Australia. The company announced on Monday night that it had bought a 20 percent stake in Fairfax Holdings in a deal worth $506 million. NZ First leader Winston Peters on Monday defended his party's new ministers as criticism persisted that the new Cabinet was inexperienced, male-dominated and under-represented the South Island. "I chose them because I know they're all up to the task," Peters said after the swearing in ceremony at Government House. Page 2.

The new government's ability to implement its agenda looked less certain on Monday night when ACT NZ leader Richard Prebble said he was unsure whether his party could support it. ACT's concerns, set to be discussed at a special caucus meeting on Tuesday, come after United NZ MP Peter Dunne has said his support for the coalition was no longer guaranteed. Page 2.

Brierley Investments has bought 20 percent of Australian media company John Fairfax Holdings in a deal worth NZ$506 million. The purchase was made through BIL's 98 percent owned listed subsidiary Australian Consolidated Investments. BIL will

also buy 18 percent of the debentures on issue. BIL executive director Rod Price said on Monday night that BIL paid A$447.1 million at an average cost per share and debenture of A$2.82. Chief executive Paul Collins said Fairfax was one of the world's premier publishing businesses. Page 15.

Air New Zealand did not discuss its recent domestic fare rise with other operators, the airline's general manager for New Zealand and Australia, Grant Lilly, said. The Commerce Commission has written "please explain" letters to Air NZ and Ansett New Zealand over their decision to raise their domestic
fares by three percent, with each rise effective on Sunday. Page 15.

New Zealand's total overseas debt rose 0.3 percent between the June and September quarters to stand at $76.4 billion at September, deputy government statistician Ian Ewing said on Monday. This was $5.7 billion or 8.1 percent higher than the corresponding time a year ago. Page 15.

Heritage Mining is confident of eventually finding enough gold for a commercially viable mine at its Onemana project on the Coromandel Peninsula. The company said on Monday it had received local authority consent two days ago to drill between 12 and 14 holes at the site. Page 15.

There should be cautious optimism in the business sector after the coalition announcement last week, helped along by lower interest rates, ANZ Bank says. As interest rates ease there will be some softening in the dollar in the next few months, the bank says in its latest Economic Focus. But a sharp
correction in the dollar of 10 percent to 15 percent is unlikely unless there is a rapid fall in inflation or substantial changes to core government policies. Page 15.
